items.prompt: Which term names learning in which a neutral stimulus comes to trigger a response after being paired with a stimulus that already triggers it?

options.label: Operant conditioning
Observational learning
Habituation
Classical conditioning

rubric: Classical conditioning is learning by pairing stimuli, as in Pavlov's dogs.
Operant conditioning is a common confusion, but it involves consequences of behavior.

items.prompt: Who is best known for proposing a hierarchy of needs, from physiological needs up to self-actualization?

options.label: Abraham Maslow
B. F. Skinner
Sigmund Freud
Jean Piaget

rubric: Maslow proposed the hierarchy of needs.
Others are linked to different theories: reinforcement, psychoanalysis, cognitive development.

items.prompt: In the Big Five model of personality, which of these is one of the five traits?

options.label: Neuroticism-free
Introversion-sensing
Conscientiousness
Dominance

rubric: Conscientiousness is one of the Big Five (OCEAN).
The other options are not Big Five trait names; introversion-sensing echoes the MBTI.

items.prompt: What is the term for the brief storage of information in memory for roughly 20-30 seconds unless it is rehearsed?

options.label: Long-term memory
Procedural memory
Short-term memory
Sensory memory

rubric: Short-term (working) memory holds information for about 20-30 seconds without rehearsal.
Sensory memory lasts only a second or so; long-term memory is durable.

items.prompt: What does the term 'placebo' refer to in a psychological experiment?

options.label: An inactive treatment given to a comparison group
The prediction about the outcome that the study tests
A real treatment that the researchers give to everyone
A questionnaire that participants complete before the study

rubric: A placebo is an inactive treatment used to control for expectations.
Other options confuse it with participants, hypotheses or measures.

items.prompt: Which of the following are stages in Piaget's theory of cognitive development? Select all that apply.

options.label: Sensorimotor
Concrete operational
Latency
Preoperational
Postconventional

rubric: Sensorimotor, preoperational and concrete operational are Piaget stages.
Postconventional is Kohlberg's; latency is Freud's.

items.prompt: A student reads a textbook chapter on the brain. The chapter says one structure is mainly involved in forming new long-term memories and is located deep in the temporal lobe. The student wants to note its name. Which structure is it?

options.label: Cerebellum
Medulla
Hippocampus
Amygdala-free cortex

rubric: The hippocampus is key to forming new explicit memories.
The cerebellum handles coordination; the medulla handles basic life functions.

items.prompt: A dog salivates at a bell that was repeatedly followed by food. In this case, what is the bell?

options.label: A negative reinforcer
A conditioned stimulus
An unconditioned stimulus
A conditioned response

rubric: The bell is a learned trigger, so a conditioned stimulus.
Food is the unconditioned stimulus; salivation to the bell is the conditioned response.

items.prompt: A child gets a sticker each time she puts her toys away, and she begins tidying more often. What does this illustrate?

options.label: Positive reinforcement
Punishment decreasing a behavior
Negative reinforcement removing a stimulus
Extinction of a learned response

rubric: Adding a pleasant stimulus that increases behavior is positive reinforcement.
Negative reinforcement removes an unpleasant stimulus; here nothing is removed.

items.prompt: Why do psychologists use random assignment in an experiment?

options.label: To pick participants so the sample matches the population
To make sure participants know which group they are in
To make groups equivalent at the start on average
To remove the need for a control group in the design

rubric: Random assignment spreads participant differences evenly across groups.
Random sampling, not assignment, is about matching the population.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the bystander effect?

options.label: People help only those who are similar to them in background
People help more when a crowd is watching them act
People are less likely to help when others are present
People help only when they expect a reward or payment

rubric: Diffusion of responsibility lowers helping when others are present.
The opposite claim reverses the effect.

items.prompt: A person says 'I'm just not a math person' after failing one test, and stops trying. Which idea from motivation research does this best fit?

options.label: An intrinsic motivation to learn
A drive reduction process
A growth mindset belief about ability
A fixed mindset belief about ability

rubric: Treating ability as unchangeable is a fixed mindset.
A growth mindset sees ability as developing with effort.

items.prompt: Which of these are examples of intrinsic motivation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Studying only to earn a cash reward from parents
Practicing guitar for the pleasure of playing
Working overtime only to avoid being fired
Reading a novel because you enjoy the story
Solving puzzles because they are fun

rubric: Intrinsic motivation comes from enjoyment of the activity itself.
Money and avoiding punishment are external, so extrinsic.

items.prompt: A friend says he feels sad and tired for most days over several weeks, has lost interest in hobbies, and sleeps poorly. A classmate says, 'He's just being lazy.' Which explanation best matches how psychology views these symptoms?

options.label: They reflect a weak character, so effort and willpower alone should fix them
They are a normal reaction to stress that fades without any outside help
They reflect a stable personality trait such as low extraversion, not a condition
They may signal depression, a treatable mental health condition

rubric: Persistent low mood and lost interest fit depression, which is treatable.
Calling it laziness ignores the clinical view; it is not a Big Five trait.

items.prompt: A child felt sharp pain during a past dentist visit. Now she feels anxious just seeing the dentist's office from the car. Which process best explains this anxiety?

options.label: Positive reinforcement of avoidance
Operant punishment of visiting behavior
Observational learning from a sibling
Classical conditioning of a fear response

rubric: The office became a conditioned stimulus paired with pain, so it now triggers fear on its own.
Operant options focus on consequences of behavior, not on a learned association between stimuli.

items.prompt: What most clearly separates negative reinforcement from punishment?

options.label: Negative reinforcement is harsher and more unpleasant than punishment
Negative reinforcement works only on animals, not on people
Negative reinforcement increases behavior; punishment decreases it
Negative reinforcement adds a stimulus; punishment removes a stimulus

rubric: Reinforcement of either kind raises the chance of a behavior; punishment lowers it.
'Negative' means removal of a stimulus, not 'bad' or 'harsh'.

items.prompt: Students often recall material better when tested in the same room where they studied it. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: The familiar room lowers anxiety, which removes interference from similar material
Memories are physically stored inside the room's objects
The room's surroundings act as retrieval cues linked to the memory
Longer study sessions in one place create stronger sensory memory traces

rubric: Context cues present at encoding help retrieval when present again.
Distractors confuse retrieval cues with sensory memory or with anxiety effects.

items.prompt: In Maslow's hierarchy, which example best illustrates a safety need?

options.label: Joining a club to feel part of a group
Pursuing art to fulfil personal potential
Looking for a steady job with benefits
Seeking a promotion to gain respect

rubric: Safety needs involve security, stability and protection from harm.
The others describe belonging, esteem and self-actualization needs.

items.prompt: Maria sees a driver cut her off and thinks, 'What a rude person,' without considering that he might be rushing to a hospital. Which concept does this show?

options.label: Diffusion of responsibility among drivers
Self-serving bias in judging her own driving
Confirmation bias in searching for evidence
Fundamental attribution error in judging others

rubric: She explains his behavior by disposition and overlooks situational causes.
Self-serving bias concerns explaining one's own outcomes, not other people's.

items.prompt: Which of the following are dimensions of the Big Five model of personality, as opposed to other psychological constructs? Select all that apply.

options.label: Locus of control
Agreeableness
Openness to experience
Intelligence
Neuroticism

rubric: Openness, agreeableness, neuroticism, conscientiousness and extraversion make up the Big Five.
Intelligence and locus of control are separate constructs.

items.prompt: A news story reports that people who sleep fewer hours also report more anxiety. A reader concludes that losing sleep must be causing anxiety. A psychology student reviews the claim. What is the most accurate interpretation of the finding?

options.label: The link shows that anxiety causes poor sleep, because anxious people lie awake worrying and so sleep less
The link shows association only; anxiety might cause poor sleep, or a third factor might drive both
Because the sample was large, the causal claim is confirmed, since big samples remove any doubt about cause
Because sleep and anxiety were self-reported, the data are unreliable and no relationship can exist

rubric: A correlation alone cannot show direction or rule out third variables.
Distractors swap in a different causal claim or dismiss the data entirely.

items.prompt: A salesperson earns a bonus after every 10th sale, regardless of how long it takes. Which reinforcement schedule is this?

options.label: Fixed-ratio
Variable-interval
Fixed-interval
Variable-ratio

rubric: Reward after a set number of responses is a fixed-ratio schedule.
Variable-ratio would vary the count; interval schedules depend on elapsed time.

items.prompt: A 4-year-old watches water poured from a short wide glass into a tall narrow one. Using Piaget's theory, what is she most likely to say?

options.label: Both glasses hold the same amount of water
The amount is unknown until the water is measured exactly
She cannot say anything because she lacks object permanence
The tall glass has more water because it looks taller

rubric: Preoperational children typically fail conservation tasks and judge by appearance.
Sameness answers reflect the concrete operational stage.

items.prompt: A person collapses on a busy city sidewalk with dozens of pedestrians nearby. Based on bystander research, what is the most likely result?

options.label: Help is faster because crowds raise group conformity to norms
Help is faster because each person feels watched and more accountable
Help is slower because each onlooker assumes someone else will act
Help depends mainly on each passerby's personal kindness, not on crowd size

rubric: Diffusion of responsibility lowers the chance that any one bystander acts.
Distractors ignore the situational effect of group size.

items.prompt: Dev paid a very high fee for a gym that turned out to be mediocre. According to cognitive dissonance theory, what is he most likely to say?

options.label: I never actually wanted to exercise anyway
The gym is actually great and worth every penny
This gym was a waste of money and I regret it
Most gyms are about the same in quality and price

rubric: He reduces the clash between a costly choice and a poor result by upgrading his view of the gym.
Regret would leave the dissonance unresolved.

items.prompt: Which situation is an example of positive punishment?

options.label: A worker is praised after finishing a report early
A teen is given extra chores after breaking curfew
A teen loses phone access after breaking curfew
A driver stops speeding to avoid a nagging alarm

rubric: Positive punishment adds an unpleasant consequence to reduce a behavior.
Losing phone access removes a pleasant stimulus, which is negative punishment.

items.prompt: Which situations are examples of classical conditioning? Select all that apply.

options.label: Copying a sibling's way of tying shoes
Feeling nauseous at the smell of a food that once caused food poisoning
Studying harder after a teacher praises good grades
Heart racing at the sound of a drill after a painful dental visit

rubric: Both involve a neutral stimulus acquiring a response through association.
Praise is operant reinforcement and copying a sibling is observational learning.

items.prompt: Lena has an exam in five days and wants to remember as much as possible long-term. She can read her notes for five hours the night before, or spread her study out. Applying research on memory, which plan is best?

options.label: Study one hour the night before, then reread the notes again at dawn
Study five hours straight the night before, with no breaks at all
Read all notes once on day one, then avoid them until the exam to avoid confusion
Study 40 minutes daily across five days, quizzing herself each time

rubric: Spaced practice with retrieval testing produces stronger long-term retention.
Cramming and a single reading give weaker retention.

items.prompt: After a bout of food poisoning from shrimp salad, Dana now feels nauseated whenever she sees shrimp. In classical conditioning terms, what is the conditioned stimulus?

options.label: The shrimp salad she ate while sick
The illness caused by the bacteria
The sight of shrimp
The nausea she feels when she sees shrimp

rubric: The sight of shrimp was neutral, was paired with illness, and now triggers nausea, so it is the CS.
Distractors confuse the CS with the conditioned response (nausea at the sight) or the unconditioned stimulus (illness).

items.prompt: A manager wants employees to keep submitting ideas long after bonuses end. Which reinforcement schedule for the bonuses should she use to make the behavior most resistant to extinction?

options.label: Fixed-interval: a bonus on the last Friday of each month, whatever the number of ideas
Fixed-ratio: a bonus after every 5 ideas, so effort maps directly onto reward
Variable-ratio: a bonus after an unpredictable number of ideas
Continuous: a bonus after every single idea, so the link is as clear as possible

rubric: Variable-ratio schedules produce the most persistent behavior because reward timing is unpredictable.
Continuous reinforcement extinguishes fastest once rewards stop; fixed schedules are easier to detect.

items.prompt: A student has 6 study hours available for an exam in three weeks. Based on research on memory, which plan will most likely give the best long-term retention?

options.label: Reread the textbook three times the night before the exam
Spread the hours over several days, rereading and highlighting each chapter
Copy notes word for word in one sitting, then rest until the exam
Spread the hours over several days, using self-quizzing on each topic

rubric: Spaced practice combined with retrieval practice strengthens long-term memory.
Cramming, rereading and highlighting feel productive but give weaker retention.

items.prompt: A 5-year-old watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass. Using Piaget's theory, what will the child most likely say?

options.label: The amounts are equal because nothing was added or removed
The amounts are equal only if the water is poured back
The tall glass has less because its container is narrower
The tall glass has more because the water level looks higher

rubric: Preoperational children lack conservation and focus on one salient feature, here height.
Saying amounts are equal reflects concrete operational reasoning, which the child has not yet reached.

items.prompt: Sam knows regular smoking is harmful but keeps smoking. Which statement by Sam is the clearest example of reducing cognitive dissonance?

options.label: "I feel anxious every time I read about lung disease."
"I plan to quit next year, after a patch is prescribed."
"My doctor told me that smoking is harmful to me."
"Smoking relaxes me, and stress is bad for health too."

rubric: Dissonance is reduced by adding a justification that makes the conflicting behavior seem acceptable.
Other options describe a future plan, an emotion or a fact, not a change in cognition to ease the conflict.

items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of negative reinforcement? Select all that apply.

options.label: A child cleans his room to stop his mother's nagging, and cleans more often
A child is scolded for hitting, and hits less often
A parent takes away a teen's phone after shouting, and the shouting declines
A driver buckles up to stop the beeping, and buckles up more reliably
Taking aspirin ends a headache, so the person takes aspirin more often

rubric: Negative reinforcement removes an unpleasant stimulus and so increases the behavior.
Taking a phone away is negative punishment, and scolding is positive punishment; both reduce behavior.

items.prompt: A man collapses on a crowded train platform. Dozens of commuters glance at him but no one moves, each assuming someone else will act. If he regains enough awareness to call out, which action best applies research on the bystander effect?

options.label: Stay silent and wait until a security guard happens by
Ask the whole crowd whether anyone happens to be a doctor
Point at one person and say, "You in the red coat, call 911"
Shout "Help!" as loudly as possible and keep repeating it to everyone nearby

rubric: Assigning a specific person counters diffusion of responsibility.
General appeals leave responsibility spread across the crowd, so each person still assumes someone else will act.

items.prompt: A city finds that weeks with higher ice cream sales also have more drownings. What is the best analysis of this correlation?

options.label: A third variable, hot weather, likely raises both swimming and ice cream sales
The correlation is too weak to reflect anything real, so it can be ignored
Ice cream causes cramps that lead to drowning, so sales should be limited
Drownings cause grief eating, which raises ice cream sales

rubric: A confounding variable, temperature, plausibly drives both measures.
Other options assert a direct causal link or dismiss a pattern without examining its source.

items.prompt: A manager concludes that an employee who arrived 30 minutes late is lazy. She later learns the subway line was shut down all morning. Which error did her original judgment most likely involve?

options.label: Confirmation bias, because she interpreted the lateness as support for a belief that the employee was lazy
The fundamental attribution error, by overlooking the situational cause of the lateness
The halo effect, because she judged the employee on one good trait
Self-serving bias, crediting herself for her own punctuality

rubric: The fundamental attribution error is overweighting disposition and underweighting situational factors.
The other biases involve self-credit, selective evidence or generalizing from a positive trait, none of which is described.

items.prompt: Researchers let 100 patients choose whether to join a new therapy or a waiting list. The therapy group improves more. What is the main flaw in concluding the therapy works?

options.label: Self-selection: those who chose therapy may differ in motivation
The sample of 100 is too small to detect a difference between the groups
Waiting-list patients may improve through expectation alone, which inflates the control group's scores
Improvement was probably judged by the clinician, who knew which patients had received therapy

rubric: Without random assignment, preexisting differences such as motivation can explain the outcome.
Sample size, placebo and measurement are not the central flaw in this design.

items.prompt: A witness saw a car pass a stop sign. After an officer asked, "How fast was the car going when it smashed the stop sign?", she later recalls broken glass that was never there. Which principle best explains this?

options.label: Flashbulb memories are recorded accurately but retrieved in the wrong order
Her encoding was too shallow, so nothing was stored about the scene
Retroactive interference from later events erased the original memory of the accident
Memory is reconstructive, so later information can alter what is recalled

rubric: The misinformation effect shows that leading wording can be incorporated into reconstructed memories.
Interference and shallow encoding do not explain a newly added false detail.

items.prompt: Children who loved drawing were promised prizes for drawing. Weeks later, once prizes stopped, they drew far less than children never rewarded. Which is the best explanation?

options.label: The children outgrew drawing at the same moment, a developmental coincidence
Drawing was punished once the prizes stopped, so it became aversive
External rewards undermined their intrinsic motivation, the overjustification effect
Classical conditioning linked drawing with the prizes, which then disappeared

rubric: Extrinsic rewards for an already enjoyed activity can shift motivation from internal to external.
Conditioning, punishment or coincidence do not account for lower interest compared with the unrewarded group.

items.prompt: A study of 200 college psychology students using self-report surveys claims its findings describe "how people behave." Which are valid criticisms of that claim? Select all that apply.

options.label: Self-reports can be distorted by social desirability, so answers may not match behavior
The findings must be false because students cannot be studied
A sample of 200 can never support any conclusion at all
Undergraduates from one school may not represent people of other ages and cultures

rubric: Sample representativeness and self-report bias both limit generalizability and validity.
Students can be studied, and 200 can support cautious conclusions; these options overstate the problem.

items.prompt: A study finds that identical twins raised apart have IQ scores that are much more similar than those of unrelated people raised apart. A commentator says this proves that upbringing does not matter for intelligence. Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: The claim holds, because if twins match so closely, genes must fully determine IQ and the environment adds nothing
Genes plausibly matter, but heritability describes variation in a group, not an absence of environmental effects
The claim fails, because twin studies can only measure personality traits and cannot be applied to cognitive abilities
The claim fails, because twins raised apart almost always end up in identical environments, so the similarity is purely environmental

rubric: Heritability is a population-level statistic and does not mean the environment is irrelevant for an individual.
Other options overstate genetic determinism or make false claims about twin studies.

items.prompt: A survey finds that heavy social media users report more loneliness. Which additional evidence would best help separate "use increases loneliness" from "lonely people turn to social media more"?

options.label: Repeated measures of both variables over months, showing whether earlier use predicts later loneliness more than the reverse
The same association replicated after separating participants by age and gender, showing no subgroup differs
A more precise usage measure from phone logs, showing the association is stronger than self-reports suggested
A much larger one-time survey drawn from many countries, showing the same association appears across cultures

rubric: Only data tracking both variables over time can show which one tends to precede change in the other.
The other options strengthen or generalise the correlation but leave its direction unresolved.

items.prompt: On a fixed-interval schedule (a reward for the first response after 60 seconds), an animal pauses after each reward and responds faster as the interval ends. Which analysis best explains the pause?

options.label: It learns that responses just after a reward never pay off, so responding rises only near the interval's end
It gets physically tired after each reward, and its response rate returns once it has recovered enough energy to continue
It forgets the contingency after every reward, and has to relearn it again before responding at a steady pace
It is satiated by the reward itself, so motivation falls and then rebuilds with a time-based hunger cycle

rubric: Temporal discrimination of the schedule produces the post-reinforcement pause and scalloped pattern.
Fatigue, forgetting and satiation do not predict a pattern tied to the interval's timing.

items.prompt: A witness was never shown a yield sign at a crash scene. A week later, after an interviewer's question mentioned a yield sign, she confidently describes seeing one. Which memory process best accounts for this?

options.label: Repression: the original scene was pushed out of awareness because it was distressing, and the gap was filled
Proactive interference: older knowledge of road signs blocked her from encoding what actually happened at the scene
Simple decay: the original trace faded with time, so she guessed the missing detail with no outside influence
Source misattribution: information from the later interview was stored and mistaken for part of the original event

rubric: Post-event information was incorporated and its source misattributed, which is the misinformation effect.
Decay and repression do not explain the specific detail supplied by the interviewer.

items.prompt: A manager, knowing nothing about an employee's commute, calls the employee's lateness a sign of laziness. When the manager is late, she blames traffic. Which analysis best fits this pattern?

options.label: Confirmation bias alone: she searched for evidence of laziness after already deciding that the employee was lazy
Cognitive dissonance: she must resolve a conflict between believing she is punctual and arriving late herself
Actor-observer asymmetry: others' behaviour is read dispositionally while one's own is read through the situation
Self-serving bias alone: she credits herself for successes and blames others only when outcomes turn out badly

rubric: The contrast between dispositional explanations for others and situational ones for self is the actor-observer pattern.
The other options name real biases but do not capture the self-versus-other difference described.

items.prompt: Two siblings experience the same family upheaval. One develops major depression and the other does not. Which framework best explains the difference?

options.label: Diathesis-stress: a stressor produces disorder mainly in those whose predispositions make them more vulnerable to it
Social learning only: the sibling who became depressed simply copied a parent's way of expressing sadness
Fixed-biology: genes alone determine who becomes depressed, so the stressor played no real part in the outcome
Behaviourist: the stressor itself acts as a punisher, so each sibling's mood should fall equally in proportion to it

rubric: Diathesis-stress holds that vulnerability and stress interact, so the same stress yields different outcomes.
The distractors treat the cause as stress alone, genes alone or imitation alone, ignoring the interaction.

items.prompt: A company reports that employees who played a "brain training" game for a month improved their memory test scores, and credits the game. Which problems weaken that causal claim? Select all that apply.

options.label: A standardised test was used, which makes any measured change unreliable by design
All participants were adults, so no result from the study can be interpreted at all
There was no control group, so gains may reflect practice on the memory test itself
Volunteers expected improvement, which can raise effort and scores regardless of the game
Employees with unusually low first scores tend to score nearer average when retested

rubric: Practice effects, expectancy and regression to the mean each offer rival explanations for the gain.
Using adults or a standardised test limits generalisation or nothing; it does not confound the causal claim.

items.prompt: A school gives pizza coupons to children who read ten books. During the program, reading rises. Months after it ends, children who were previously enthusiastic readers read less than they did before it began. Which analysis best explains the drop?

options.label: Habituation: after many books, reading stopped being novel to the children, so their interest fell no matter how it was rewarded
Learned helplessness: failing to earn enough coupons convinced many children that their effort had no effect on outcomes
Extinction: once the coupons stopped, the reinforced reading behaviour decayed, falling off as the learned reward link faded
Overjustification: the reward shifted their explanation of reading from interest to payment, weakening intrinsic motivation

rubric: An expected external reward can undermine existing intrinsic motivation, as the overjustification effect predicts.
Extinction would return behaviour to baseline, not below it, and the other options do not fit the described pattern.

items.prompt: A tutoring company claims students learn best when taught in their preferred "learning style" (visual, auditory, kinesthetic). Judged by research standards, which critique is strongest?

options.label: Controlled studies rarely show that matching instruction to a preferred style improves outcomes over mismatched instruction
Learning style questionnaires are too short, so the claim would hold once a longer inventory is designed for them
Students differ in style, so the claim is correct but needs bigger classes to be seen in the data clearly
Visual material is always superior, so teaching to the auditory or kinesthetic preferences would harm learners

rubric: The claim depends on a matching effect, and experiments testing it generally fail to find one.
Other options accept the premise or replace it with an equally unsupported universal claim.

items.prompt: Researchers want evidence on whether less sleep causes worse exam performance. Criteria: causal inference, ethical acceptability, and feasibility. Which design best balances them?

options.label: Randomly assign volunteers to a mildly shortened or normal sleep schedule for several nights, then test them
Deprive volunteers of all sleep for several days, then compare them with a group who sleep normally
Interview high-scoring and low-scoring students about their sleep habits and look for themes in their answers
Survey thousands of students about sleep and grades, then control statistically for study time and age

rubric: Random assignment supports causal claims, and a mild manipulation keeps risk acceptable.
Surveys and interviews cannot rule out confounds, and total deprivation is ethically unacceptable.

items.prompt: A clinic must choose a first-line treatment for an adult with a specific phobia of flying. Criteria: strong evidence of effectiveness, a short course, and a direct focus on the fear. Which is the best choice?

options.label: Supportive talk therapy, offering empathy and reflection while avoiding any contact with feared situations
Graded exposure therapy, with repeated, planned contact with flying-related cues until fear responses decline
Daily benzodiazepines, reducing arousal for as long as the person continues to take the medication
Long-term psychoanalysis, uncovering unconscious childhood conflicts that are assumed to underlie the fear

rubric: Exposure has strong evidence for specific phobias and works within a few sessions.
The others lack comparable evidence, are lengthy, or let avoidance or medication maintain the fear.

items.prompt: A documentary says the Stanford prison experiment proves that situations alone turn ordinary people cruel. Which critique best judges this conclusion?

options.label: Guards were coached and participants knew what was expected, so demand characteristics limit what the study can show
The results are discredited because any study involving role-play is automatically worthless as psychological evidence
The study used a sample that was too large, so small differences between participants were treated as meaningful
The study measured behaviour in a laboratory, and lab studies of behaviour can never say anything about people

rubric: Evidence of coaching and demand characteristics weakens the claim that the situation alone caused the cruelty.
The other critiques are overgeneralised or do not match the study's actual weaknesses.

items.prompt: A student has three weeks to prepare for a cumulative exam and wants the most durable retention. Criteria: evidence-backed, and workable alongside other courses. Which plan is best?

options.label: Rereading and highlighting the textbook chapters twice, finishing them the weekend before the exam
Copying lecture notes neatly each evening, so that the summaries are organised and easy to review later
Short daily sessions of self-testing on all material, revisiting older topics at widening gaps
One long session each weekend, covering a single topic at a time in great depth until it feels mastered

rubric: Retrieval practice with spacing produces better long-term retention than passive review.
Rereading, massed study and copying notes feel productive but yield weaker durable learning.

items.prompt: A pundit says, "IQ is fixed at birth by genes, so nothing can change it." Which critiques are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: IQ tests predict nothing about later outcomes, so the debate over fixedness is meaningless to have
Twin studies show intelligence has no genetic component, so genes play no role in score differences
Heritability describes variation across a population, not how fixed any one person's score is
Average test scores have risen across generations, which a purely fixed genetic account struggles to explain
Children moved into enriched environments often show score gains, so environment can shift scores

rubric: Heritability is a population statistic, and score gains across generations and environments show scores are not fixed.
Claiming zero genetic influence or zero predictive value is as unsupported as the pundit's claim.

items.prompt: A firm wants to reduce bias in hiring. Criteria: measurable effect on hiring decisions, modest cost, and no reliance on managers' self-awareness. HR proposes four options. Which best meets all three criteria?

options.label: Posting a diversity statement on the careers page, so applicants see the firm values fairness in hiring
Structured interviews: the same questions for every candidate, scored against a predefined rubric
A one-day implicit bias workshop, followed by managers' pledges to treat every candidate fairly
Letting interviewers rely on gut feelings, which are trusted to reflect subtle signs of fit with the team

rubric: Structured interviews with rubrics constrain discretion, reduce bias and are cheap to measure.
One-off workshops and statements rely on awareness or intent, and gut feelings can carry bias.

items.prompt: A commentator claims Milgram's obedience studies prove that ordinary people are inherently cruel. Judged against the full set of Milgram's variations, which evaluation is best supported?

options.label: Strong claim: the effect appeared across many variations, which shows obedience stays constant whatever the situation looks like
Weak claim: obedience fell sharply when the victim was close or the authority was remote, so situational features explain much of the variation
Weak claim: because participants were debriefed afterwards, the obedience seen was not real behavior and the results lack all validity
Strong claim: since 65% reached the maximum shock, most people evidently carry a stable sadistic trait that authority simply releases

rubric: Variations showed obedience depends heavily on situational features, which undercuts a fixed-disposition reading.
Distractors treat one headline figure as a trait, or wrongly dismiss the data because of debriefing.

items.prompt: You must judge which result would best support the claim that matching teaching to a learner's preferred style improves learning. Which finding is the strongest evidence?

options.label: Learners randomly assigned to formats scored higher when matched to their style than mismatched, with the reverse for the other group
Most students named the same preferred style on a questionnaire completed twice a month apart, showing stable and consistent self-reports
Learners enjoyed lessons more and rated them as more helpful when taught in their preferred style, regardless of their later test scores
Visual learners scored higher overall than auditory learners on a map memory test, across every teaching format used in the study

rubric: The matching hypothesis predicts a crossover interaction between style and format on learning outcomes.
Distractors show enjoyment, main effects or reliability of self-report, none of which test matching.

items.prompt: An employer chooses between the Big Five inventory and a four-letter type test for hiring. Criteria: stable scores on retest and evidence of predicting job performance. Which judgement is best?

options.label: The type test is better because it has stronger evidence of stable results, since people rarely change how they answer on retest
Both are equal because any questionnaire answered honestly measures the same underlying traits whatever its scoring format
The Big Five is better because its traits show retest stability and modest prediction of job performance
The type test is better because sorting people into discrete types makes results simpler to communicate and so more predictive

rubric: Big Five dimensions have supporting reliability and predictive validity evidence, while dichotomous types often change on retest.
Distractors confuse ease of communication or format with validity.

items.prompt: An original ego-depletion study (n = 40, p = .04) found a sizeable effect. A large preregistered multi-lab replication then found an effect near zero. Which conclusion is best warranted?

options.label: The failed replication suggests self-control may be a poorly defined construct, so the whole line of research should be set aside
The original effect was probably inflated by small samples and flexible analysis, so the claim should be held with strong doubt
The replication is probably less trustworthy because the original study came first and established the effect, so later work should count for less
Both results are probably valid, so the effect likely depends on features of the original laboratory that the multi-lab design did not capture

rubric: Large preregistered replications carry more weight than small underpowered originals with a marginal p-value.
Distractors appeal to priority of discovery or overgeneralise to the whole field.

items.prompt: A police department wants to cut false identifications of innocent suspects without losing many correct ones, at low cost. Which reform is the best judgement?

options.label: Telling witnesses the culprit is definitely present so they take the task seriously and choose carefully from the lineup
Having an officer unaware of the suspect run the lineup with fair fillers and record the witness's confidence immediately
Using hypnosis before the lineup to retrieve a clearer memory of the face, which improves accuracy of later identification
Showing the witness the same lineup several times so that repeated viewing builds the confidence needed for a reliable choice

rubric: Double-blind administration prevents cueing and early confidence records are more diagnostic of accuracy.
Distractors increase suggestion or pressure to choose, or rely on unreliable hypnosis.

items.prompt: A textbook claims a finding reveals a human universal, yet all samples were from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, democratic societies. Which are valid criticisms? Select all that apply.

options.label: Any effect found in one culture must be culturally specific, so no psychological finding could ever be general across humans
Without cross-cultural replication, a universality claim is unsupported even if the effect is strong within the sample
Random assignment inside the sample becomes invalid, so the study cannot support any causal claim even within that population
Such samples may differ from other populations on perception, fairness norms and reasoning, limiting generalisation to all humans

rubric: Narrow sampling threatens external validity and claims of universality need cross-cultural evidence.
Distractors confuse external with internal validity or overstate that nothing generalises.

items.prompt: A clinic reports that 60% of clients improved with a new therapy versus 55% with standard CBT. The new therapy's developers delivered it, clients chose their own group, and improvement was rated by the treating therapists. Which judgement is best supported?

options.label: The result is trustworthy because therapists know the clients best, so their ratings are more accurate than blinded outcome measures
The two therapies are proven equal because the gap is small, and small gaps always indicate that no real difference exists
The new therapy is clearly superior because a higher improvement rate in a real clinic is more valid than a laboratory trial
The five-point gap is uninterpretable because self-selection, developer allegiance and unblinded ratings could each produce it

rubric: Self-selection, allegiance and unblinded assessment are confounds that make the comparison uninformative.
Distractors overvalue ecological setting or insider ratings, or treat a small gap as proof of equality.

items.prompt: You must design a test of whether a new mnemonic improves word-list recall, ruling out differences in effort, time and scorer expectation. Which design meets all three constraints?

options.label: Assign the mnemonic to a high-scoring group and no strategy to a low-scoring group, then compare their gains on the recall lists
Randomly assign participants to the mnemonic or an equal-time alternative strategy, and have scorers blind to condition mark the recall lists
Test each participant first with no strategy and later with the mnemonic, comparing the two scores while you score all the recall lists yourself afterwards
Give the mnemonic to volunteers who requested training and compare them with classmates who did not, scoring every list yourself

rubric: Random assignment, an active equal-time control and blinded scoring address motivation, time and expectancy.
Distractors keep self-selection, order effects or regression to the mean.

items.prompt: Ethics boards forbid assigning teenagers to increase social media use. You want causal evidence on whether heavy use raises loneliness. Which design best fits this constraint?

options.label: Interview the loneliest teens about their habits and look for common themes in their reports about social media
Randomly assign heavy users to either limit their use for several weeks or continue as usual, measuring loneliness before and after
Compare countries' average social media use with national loneliness rates and treat the relationship as evidence of causation
Survey a large sample once and statistically control for age and gender, then report the correlation as a causal estimate

rubric: Randomly assigning reduction in use permits causal inference without ethically problematic exposure.
Distractors rely on correlational or selected data, which cannot isolate cause.

items.prompt: A trainer wants a new habit, once learned, to persist as long as possible after rewards stop. Which reinforcement plan best meets this goal?

options.label: Reward every single response throughout training so the learner links action and reward perfectly, then stop the rewards entirely
Begin with continuous reinforcement to establish the habit, then gradually thin to an unpredictable variable-ratio schedule
Reward only the first response each day, since limiting rewards keeps the habit scarce and valued once rewards are removed
Switch to punishing missed responses once the habit is learned, as aversive consequences keep it strong after the rewards stop

rubric: Variable schedules after initial acquisition produce strong resistance to extinction.
Distractors keep continuous reinforcement, which extinguishes fast, or add punishment.

items.prompt: A firm proposes using a new personality questionnaire for hiring, citing high internal consistency and staff comments that it was insightful. Which evidence is most essential to add before the questionnaire is used to select applicants?

options.label: A longer version of the questionnaire, since adding items raises internal consistency and so its predictive power for hiring
Evidence that scores predict later job performance in a validation sample, showing the test measures what hiring needs
Ratings from a larger group of staff that the results felt accurate, since perceived accuracy shows the test is valid for hiring
Norms split by age group, since scores are only interpretable when compared within each age band of the applicants

rubric: Reliability and face validity do not show the test predicts performance; criterion validity is needed.
Distractors address length, norms or perceived accuracy instead of predictive validity.

items.prompt: A lecturer wants students to retain course content for a year, with limited class time and no extra tests. Which plan best meets these constraints?

options.label: Highlight key terms in the textbook during lectures, because highlighting repeated across weeks makes the content stick
Ask students to reread notes in one long block before the final exam, because immersion yields the strongest memory traces
Embed short low-stakes retrieval quizzes with feedback across the term, mixing earlier topics into later sessions
Give summary handouts at the end, since concise material reduces study time and so retention after a long delay

rubric: Spaced, interleaved retrieval practice with feedback produces durable retention and fits within class time.
Distractors are rereading, handouts and highlighting, which are weak learning strategies.

items.prompt: You are designing a campus campaign to reduce the bystander effect in emergencies. Which elements belong in a plan grounded in research? Select all that apply.

options.label: Encourage students to wait for others to react first, since reading the crowd shows whether help is needed
Teach students that responsibility diffuses in groups, so each person should assume they may be the one needed
Train people to direct a named individual, such as "you in the red coat, call emergency services"
Practise brief role-plays of intervening so that action steps are rehearsed before an emergency happens
Tell students that larger crowds are safer because someone else will surely already have called for help

rubric: Diffusion of responsibility is reduced by awareness, direct assignment of tasks and rehearsed responses.
Distractors reinforce pluralistic ignorance and the assumption that others will act.

items.prompt: A company wants more employees to save for retirement. Constraints: no mandates, no added cost to staff, freedom to opt out, and a fix for the inertia that keeps many from filling in forms. Which plan best meets every constraint?

options.label: Require all employees to attend a yearly seminar on compound interest, then leave enrollment as a separate form
Make enrollment compulsory with payroll deduction and no exit, so everyone saves and inertia no longer matters
Automatically enroll new hires at a default contribution rate, with a simple, easy opt-out available at any time
Email monthly reminders asking staff to open an account, with a bonus gift for those who complete the paperwork

rubric: An opt-out default uses inertia while preserving choice and costing employees nothing.
Distractors rely on education or reminders that still need action, or violate the no-mandate constraint.
